paragraphs.paraphrase: At dawn Alcinous and Odysseus get up, and Alcinous leads the way to the Phaeacians' assembly place by the ships, where the two sit side by side on a polished stone seat. Meanwhile Athena, disguised as one of Alcinous's servants, goes round the town to help Odysseus's journey home, telling people one by one to come to the assembly and hear the godlike stranger who has just arrived at the king's house after a long voyage.

barriers.quote: Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning
barriers.my_reading: A poetic way of saying 'at sunrise': Dawn is pictured as a person whose fingers are the pink streaks of first light. 'Child of morning' is odd, since dawn is the start of morning.

barriers.quote: Aldermen and town councilors of the Phaeacians
barriers.my_reading: The Phaeacian nobles and elders. Odd that Athena uses this title when she is going up to 'the citizens one by one'.
barriers.note: the stock form of address throughout (¶2, ¶6, ¶33, ¶47); modern local-government terms

paragraphs.paraphrase: Her words make everyone eager to come, and the assembly fills until every seat and all the standing room are taken. Everyone is struck by Odysseus's appearance, because Athena has made his head and shoulders more handsome and made him look taller and more powerfully built, so that he will impress the Phaeacians and do well in the contests they will challenge him to; then Alcinous speaks.

barriers.quote: taller and stouter
barriers.my_reading: Bigger and more powerfully built, not fatter.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Alcinous tells the Phaeacian leaders that this unknown stranger has come to his house from somewhere, east or west, and wants a passage home arranged; they should provide it as they have for others, since no visitor has ever complained of being sent off too slowly. He orders a brand-new ship launched and crewed by fifty-two of the best young sailors, who are to fix their oars at their seats and then come to the palace for a feast he will provide. The leaders are to join him in entertaining the guest in the hall, no excuses accepted, with the incomparable singer Demodocus to perform.

barriers.quote: He wants an escort
barriers.my_reading: He wants to be taken home by ship; 'escort' means a passage with a crew, not a companion or guard.

barriers.quote: when you have made fast your oars each by his own seat
barriers.my_reading: Each rower ties his oar in place beside his rowing bench so the ship is ready to go.

barriers.quote: I will find you in everything
barriers.my_reading: I will provide everything you need (food and drink), not 'I will come and find you'.

barriers.quote: I am giving these instructions to the young men who will form the crew
barriers.my_reading: Only after the fact do we learn that the oar instructions were for the young crew and the next orders are for the elders; until this sentence it sounds as if he is telling the councilors to row.

barriers.quote: in the gallery
barriers.my_reading: The palace hall where they feast (it has pillars, ¶43), not an art gallery or a balcony.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Alcinous leads the way while a servant fetches Demodocus; the fifty-two rowers launch the ship, put its mast and sails on board, tie the oars to their pegs with leather straps, spread the sails, anchor a little offshore and then go to the palace. The palace buildings and grounds fill with crowds of men young and old, and Alcinous has twelve sheep, eight grown pigs and two oxen slaughtered for them, skinned and prepared for a grand feast.

barriers.quote: bound the oars to the thole pins with twisted thongs of leather
barriers.my_reading: Tied the oars with twisted leather straps to pegs on the ship's side that the oars pivot against.
barriers.note: 'thole pins' unknown to most readers; 'thongs' has a modern clothing sense

barriers.quote: all the precincts
barriers.my_reading: The palace grounds and enclosures, not a police precinct or district.

barriers.quote: Alcinous killed them a dozen sheep
barriers.my_reading: He slaughtered twelve sheep (and the pigs and oxen) for them to eat.
barriers.note: first pass reads 'killed them', i.e. the men

barriers.quote: skinned and dressed
barriers.my_reading: Skinned and butchered the carcasses ready for cooking; nothing to do with clothes.

paragraphs.paraphrase: A servant brings in the famous singer Demodocus, whom the Muse loved but gave both good and bad: a divine gift of song, and blindness. Pontonous sets his chair among the guests against a pillar, hangs his lyre on a peg above his head and guides his hands to where he can feel for it, and puts a table beside him with a basket of food and a cup of wine to drink whenever he likes.

barriers.quote: presently
barriers.my_reading: Soon, after a while (not 'currently').

paragraphs.paraphrase: When the guests have eaten and drunk their fill, the Muse moves Demodocus to sing of heroes' deeds, in particular a story famous at the time: the quarrel in which Odysseus and Achilles hurled fierce words at each other at a feast. Their leader Agamemnon was glad to hear his chiefs quarrel, because Apollo had predicted it to him when he consulted the oracle at Pytho; this was the beginning of the disaster Zeus brought on both the Danaans and the Trojans.

barriers.quote: But Agamemnon was glad when he heard his chieftains quarreling
barriers.my_reading: He seems glad because the quarrel fulfilled a prophecy, but the text never says what the prophecy promised or why a quarrel among his own chiefs would be good news.
barriers.note: outside knowledge only (the prophecy tied the quarrel to the fall of Troy)

barriers.quote: at Pytho when he crossed the stone floor to consult the oracle
barriers.my_reading: At a shrine called Pytho, where Agamemnon went in over its stone threshold to ask the god for a prophecy.

barriers.quote: fell upon Danaans and Trojans alike
barriers.my_reading: The Danaans must be the Greeks, the other side in the war against Troy.
barriers.note: the Greeks are later also called Achaeans and Argives; none of these names is explained

paragraphs.paraphrase: While the singer sings, Odysseus pulls his purple cloak over his head to hide his face, ashamed to let the Phaeacians see him cry; each time the song pauses he wipes his eyes, uncovers his face and pours a drink offering, but when they urge Demodocus on he covers his head and weeps bitterly again. Only Alcinous, sitting beside him, notices his heavy sighs, and at once tells the leaders they have had enough of feast and song and should move on to athletic contests, so the guest can tell his people at home how the Phaeacians outdo everyone at boxing, wrestling, jumping and running.

barriers.quote: made a drink offering to the gods
barriers.my_reading: He pours out a little wine from his cup for the gods as a ritual; what exactly is done is not explained.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Alcinous leads everyone out; a servant hangs Demodocus's lyre on its peg, leads him out of the hall and sets him on the road with the Phaeacian leaders going to the games, followed by thousands of people. Many fine athletes compete, listed by name, among them Euryalus, godlike as Ares and the best-looking Phaeacian after Laodamas, and three of Alcinous's sons, Laodamas, Halios and Clytoneus.

barriers.quote: There were Acroneos, Ocyalus, Elatreus
barriers.my_reading: A roll-call of thirteen competitors, most of whom never appear again; there is no way to tell which names matter.

barriers.quote: who was like Ares himself
barriers.my_reading: He looked like a god, apparently one known for strength or looks; only later (¶18) does the Book show that Ares is a god.
barriers.note: Ares as god of war is outside knowledge only

paragraphs.paraphrase: The footrace comes first: the runners start together from the post and raise dust across the plain, and Clytoneus wins by a huge margin, the length of the strip a pair of mules plows. Euryalus wins the wrestling, Amphialus the jumping, Elatreus the discus and Laodamas the boxing. Then Laodamas proposes asking the stranger if he is good at any sport, since he looks enormously strong in thighs, calves, hands and neck and is not old, though his recent suffering at sea may have worn him down.

barriers.quote: the length of the furrow a couple of mules can plow in a fallow field
barriers.my_reading: A big lead, as long as the strip of ground a pair of mules plows; the actual distance is hard to picture.

barriers.quote: when they had all been diverted with the games
barriers.my_reading: When they had all enjoyed themselves at the games ('diverted' = entertained, not redirected).

paragraphs.paraphrase: Euryalus agrees and tells Laodamas to go and put it to the guest himself.

Laodamas goes into the middle of the crowd and politely invites Odysseus to enter one of the contests, assuming he has competed often, since nothing brings a man more lasting credit than proving himself with hands and feet. He urges him to try, forget his sorrows and not worry about delay, because the ship is already launched and the crew chosen.
Odysseus asks why Laodamas is taunting him: after endless suffering his mind is on his troubles, not contests, and he is here as a suppliant begging the king and people to help him home.

barriers.quote: why do you taunt me like this?
barriers.my_reading: He takes the pressure to compete while he is grieving and worn out as a provocation, although Laodamas's invitation sounded polite.

barriers.quote: praying your king and his people
barriers.my_reading: Begging the king and people, not praying to them as gods.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Euryalus openly insults him: evidently he is no good at any of the usual sports and must be one of those greedy merchant sea-captains who think of nothing but their cargoes out and back, with nothing of the athlete about him.

barriers.quote: reviled him outright
barriers.my_reading: Openly insulted him.

barriers.quote: one of those grasping traders
barriers.my_reading: An insult to his status: he is being called a greedy commoner who trades for profit rather than a gentleman who competes in sport.
barriers.note: the assumption that trade is beneath a nobleman is left implicit

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus angrily calls Euryalus insolent and says the gods don't give every man looks, eloquence and sense together: one man is unimpressive to look at but speaks so pleasingly and modestly that people follow and honor him, while another is as handsome as a god but has no sense, which is Euryalus's case. Euryalus's thoughtless words have enraged him and are wrong, since he is skilled at many sports and was one of the best athletes of his day when young, though now worn out by war and hardship at sea. Still, stung by the taunts, he will compete.

barriers.quote: So true is it that the gods do not grace all men alike in speech, person, and understanding
barriers.my_reading: It really is true that the gods don't give every man everything: eloquence, good looks ('person') and intelligence.

barriers.quote: His honeyed moderation carries his hearers with him
barriers.my_reading: His sweet, modest way of speaking wins his listeners over.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Without even taking off his cloak, Odysseus leaps up, grabs a discus bigger and much heavier than the ones the Phaeacians use, swings it back and hurls it; it hums through the air, the Phaeacians duck as it rushes over, and it lands beyond every mark so far. Athena, disguised as a man, marks the spot and tells him even a blind man could find his mark by feeling for it, it is so far beyond the others, and no Phaeacian will come near it.

barriers.quote: The Phaeacians quailed beneath the rushing of its flight
barriers.my_reading: They cowered or ducked as the disc whizzed over them.

barriers.quote: could easily tell your mark by groping for it
barriers.my_reading: His landing mark is so far from the cluster of other marks that even a blind man feeling along the ground would find it.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Glad to find a friend in the crowd, Odysseus speaks more cheerfully: he challenges the young men to match his throw, offers to throw an even heavier disc, and in his anger will box, wrestle or run against anyone except his host Laodamas, since it is unwise for a guest abroad to challenge his host's family. He boasts that he is good at every sport and a superb archer, always first to hit an enemy, second only to Philoctetes among the Achaeans at Troy and better than any man now living, though he would not compete with great dead archers like Heracles and Eurytus, whom Apollo killed for challenging him. He can throw a spear farther than others can shoot an arrow; only in running might the Phaeacians beat him, since hunger at sea has left him weak.

barriers.quote: come up to that throw
barriers.my_reading: Match that throw.

barriers.quote: when we Achaeans were before Troy and in practice
barriers.my_reading: When the Greeks (here 'Achaeans') were besieging Troy; 'before Troy' = outside its walls, and 'and in practice' is unclear (shooting practice as opposed to battle?).
barriers.note: he also gives away here that he fought at Troy, which is easy to miss

barriers.quote: of those who still eat bread upon the face of the earth
barriers.my_reading: Of all living men, as opposed to the dead heroes he names next.

barriers.quote: Heracles, or Eurytus the Oechalian
barriers.my_reading: Great archers of the past, now dead; Heracles is presumably Hercules, and I know Eurytus only from what the text says.
barriers.note: Heracles = Hercules is outside knowledge only

barriers.quote: I can throw a dart farther than anyone else can shoot an arrow
barriers.my_reading: 'dart' = a light throwing spear or javelin, not a small darts-board dart.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Everyone is silent except Alcinous, who says they have enjoyed hearing him and understand he wants to show his ability after being offended by an athlete's rude remarks that no well-mannered person would make. He asks the guest to tell the leading men at home, when they dine with him, that the Phaeacians have inherited talents: not remarkable at boxing or wrestling, but very fast runners and superb sailors who love feasts, music, dancing, fresh clothes, warm baths and good beds. He then calls on the best dancers to perform, so the guest can report how the Phaeacians excel as sailors, runners, dancers and singers, and sends someone to fetch Demodocus's lyre from the palace.

barriers.quote: We are not particularly remarkable for our boxing, nor yet as wrestlers
barriers.my_reading: After Odysseus's display Alcinous tactfully backs away from contests they might lose and switches to what they are best at (running, sailing, dancing). It contradicts his boast in ¶6 that they surpass all nations as boxers and wrestlers.
barriers.note: the backtrack is left for the reader to notice

paragraphs.paraphrase: A servant runs for the lyre, and the nine officials chosen to run the games level the ground and mark out a wide dancing space. When the lyre arrives, Demodocus takes his place in the middle and the best young dancers dance so nimbly that Odysseus is delighted by their flashing feet.

barriers.quote: began to foot and trip it so nimbly
barriers.my_reading: Began to dance lightly and quickly.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Meanwhile the singer sings of the love affair of the gods Ares and Aphrodite, which began in the house of Hephaestus, Aphrodite's husband: Ares gave her many gifts and dishonored Hephaestus's marriage bed, and the Sun, who saw them, told Hephaestus. Furious, Hephaestus went to his forge plotting revenge and made unbreakable chains so fine that not even a god could see them, draping them all over his bedposts like cobwebs and hanging them from the ceiling beam as a trap. Then he pretended to set off for Lemnos, his favorite place, and Ares, who was watching closely, hurried to his house as soon as he saw him go, burning with desire for Aphrodite.

barriers.quote: defiled King Hephaestus’s marriage bed
barriers.my_reading: Aphrodite is Hephaestus's wife and Ares is her lover; the marriage is only implied here and confirmed in ¶21.

barriers.quote: he made as though he were setting out for the fair state of Lemnos
barriers.my_reading: He pretended to leave for Lemnos, apparently a place (island or city) he loved; 'state' is an odd word for it.

barriers.quote: But Ares kept no blind lookout
barriers.my_reading: Ares was keeping a sharp watch (his lookout was not blind), so he saw Hephaestus leave.
barriers.note: can first read as 'kept no lookout', i.e. careless, which is the opposite

paragraphs.paraphrase: Aphrodite has just come back from visiting her father Zeus and is about to sit down when Ares comes in, takes her hand and suggests they go to Hephaestus's bed, since he has gone off to Lemnos among the Sintians, whose speech is uncouth.

barriers.quote: the couch of Hephaestus
barriers.my_reading: Hephaestus's bed, not a sofa.

barriers.quote: among the Sintians, whose speech is barbarous
barriers.my_reading: The people of Lemnos, who (Ares sneers) speak a rough, foreign-sounding language.

paragraphs.paraphrase: She is more than willing, so they go to bed and are caught in the invisible net Hephaestus has laid, unable to get up or move a limb, realizing too late they are trapped. Hephaestus, who turned back before reaching Lemnos when the Sun, his spy, told him, arrives in a fury and stands in the entrance shouting to all the gods.

barriers.quote: She was nothing loath
barriers.my_reading: She was entirely willing.

barriers.quote: caught in the toils
barriers.my_reading: Caught in the net or snare of chains ('toils' = nets, not hard work).

paragraphs.paraphrase: Hephaestus calls Zeus and the other gods to come and see a ridiculous, shameful sight: Zeus's daughter Aphrodite always humiliates him because he is lame, and loves the handsome, well-built Ares, while he is crippled, which is his parents' fault for ever having him. They should see the pair asleep in his bed, a sight that enrages him; the lovers may be fond of each other, but he doubts they will want to lie there much longer or get much sleep. They will stay there, though, until her father Zeus repays the price Hephaestus paid him for his worthless daughter, who is beautiful but unfaithful.

barriers.quote: clean built
barriers.my_reading: Well-formed and straight-limbed, in contrast to Hephaestus's lameness.

barriers.quote: I do not think they will lie there longer than they can help, nor do I think they will sleep much
barriers.my_reading: Sarcasm: in love or not, now that they are trapped and on show they will not want to stay in bed, and will get no sleep.

barriers.quote: repaid me the sum I gave him
barriers.my_reading: A bride-price or marriage gifts Hephaestus paid Zeus to marry Aphrodite; the custom is not explained.

barriers.quote: his baggage of a daughter
barriers.my_reading: An insult: a shameless or worthless woman, not luggage.

barriers.quote: who is fair but not honest
barriers.my_reading: Beautiful but unfaithful ('honest' = chaste).

paragraphs.paraphrase: The gods gather at Hephaestus's house: Poseidon who encircles the earth, Hermes the bringer of luck and lord Apollo, though the goddesses stay home out of modesty. The gods stand in the doorway roaring with endless laughter at Hephaestus's cleverness, and say to one another:

barriers.quote: Earth-encircling Poseidon
barriers.my_reading: Poseidon as god of the sea, which surrounds the land.

barriers.quote: Then the givers of all good things stood in the doorway
barriers.my_reading: 'The givers of all good things' is just another name for the gods, the same ones who then laugh, not a separate group.

paragraphs.paraphrase: The gods say that wrongdoing doesn't pay and the weak can beat the strong: lame Hephaestus has caught Ares, the fastest god in heaven, and Ares will now have to pay heavy compensation.

barriers.quote: Ares will be cast in heavy damages
barriers.my_reading: Ares will be made to pay a large fine to Hephaestus, like a court ordering compensation.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Meanwhile Apollo teases Hermes, asking whether he would mind how strong the chains were if he could sleep with Aphrodite.
Hermes replies that he wishes he had the chance, even with three times as many chains and all the gods and goddesses looking on.
The gods burst out laughing, but Poseidon takes it seriously and keeps begging Hephaestus to free Ares, promising to guarantee that Ares will pay whatever compensation the gods think fair.

barriers.quote: I will undertake, as you require, that he shall pay you
barriers.my_reading: I personally guarantee that he will pay you; Poseidon offers to stand surety for Ares.
barriers.note: needed to follow the exchange about the bond in ¶27-¶28

paragraphs.paraphrase: Hephaestus refuses: a guarantee given for a bad man is worthless, and he would have no way to make Poseidon pay if Ares ran off, leaving his debts behind along with his chains.

barriers.quote: A bad man’s bond is bad security.
barriers.my_reading: A pledge made for (or by) a scoundrel is a worthless guarantee.
barriers.note: financial/legal jargon; 'bond' also suggests the chains

barriers.quote: What remedy could I enforce against you
barriers.my_reading: What could I do to make you, a powerful god, pay up?

paragraphs.paraphrase: Poseidon promises to pay the damages himself if Ares leaves without paying, and Hephaestus says that in that case he cannot and should not refuse.

Hephaestus releases the chains and the lovers dash off, Ares to Thrace and laughter-loving Aphrodite to Paphos on Cyprus, where she has a sacred grove and an altar fragrant with burnt offerings. There the Graces bathe her, rub her with the gods' own fragrant oil and dress her in lovely robes.

barriers.quote: There the Graces bathed her
barriers.my_reading: Goddesses or attendants who serve her; who the Graces are is not explained.

paragraphs.paraphrase: That is the end of the song, and Odysseus and the seafaring Phaeacians enjoyed it.

Alcinous has his sons Laodamas and Halios dance on their own, since nobody can match them. With a red ball made by Polybus, one leans back and throws it high toward the clouds and the other leaps and catches it in mid-air; then they dance while tossing it back and forth, and the young men around them cheer and stamp their feet, after which Odysseus speaks.
Odysseus tells Alcinous that his people really are the nimblest dancers in the world, as he claimed, and that he was amazed watching them.

Delighted, Alcinous tells the Phaeacian leaders that their guest has excellent judgment and deserves proper gifts of hospitality: the twelve chief men and he himself should each give a clean cloak, a shirt and a talent of fine gold, all delivered at once so the guest can enjoy his supper light-hearted. Euryalus must also make a formal apology and give a present for his rudeness.

barriers.quote: a talent of fine gold
barriers.my_reading: A set weight or amount of gold, presumably valuable; 'talent' here is a unit, not a skill.
barriers.note: how much it is worth is never given

paragraphs.paraphrase: Everyone applauds and sends servants for the presents. Euryalus tells the king he will make whatever amends are required and gives the stranger his bronze sword with a silver hilt and its newly cut ivory sheath, a valuable gift.

barriers.quote: I will give the stranger all the satisfaction you require
barriers.my_reading: I will make whatever amends you ask ('satisfaction' = compensation for an insult).

paragraphs.paraphrase: Handing Odysseus the sword, Euryalus wishes him well, hopes the winds will carry off any offensive words he said, and prays the gods grant him a safe return after his long absence and hardship.

barriers.quote: father stranger
barriers.my_reading: A respectful way to address an older man he doesn't know, roughly 'sir'.
barriers.note: sounds odd aloud; also sits a little oddly with Laodamas's remark (¶8) that he is not at all old

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus returns the good wishes and says he hopes Euryalus will never miss the sword he has given along with his apology.

barriers.quote: I hope you will not miss the sword you have given me
barriers.my_reading: A gracious reply: may you never regret giving it or need it yourself, i.e. no hard feelings; the tone could also be read as a dry dig.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus hangs the sword from his shoulder. Toward sunset the donors' servants start bringing the gifts to Alcinous's palace, where his sons receive them and hand them to their mother for safekeeping, and Alcinous leads everyone back to the palace and seats them.

barriers.quote: he girded the sword about his shoulders
barriers.my_reading: He slung the sword on its strap over his shoulder.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Alcinous tells Arete to fetch their best chest and put a clean cloak and shirt in it, to heat water in a pot on the fire for the guest's bath, and to have the Phaeacians' gifts packed carefully, so he can enjoy supper and the singing all the more. Alcinous himself will give him a beautifully made golden cup, so that he will remember him all his life whenever he pours a drink offering to Zeus or the other gods.

barriers.quote: set a copper on the fire
barriers.my_reading: Put a large copper pot or cauldron on the fire to heat water; not a coin or a policeman.
barriers.note: in ¶39 the same vessel seems to become a 'tripod'

paragraphs.paraphrase: Arete has her maids put a large three-legged cauldron full of bath water on a bright fire, feeding it sticks until the flames lick round its belly and the water heats. Meanwhile she brings a splendid chest from her own room and packs in it all the gold and clothing the Phaeacians have given, adding last a cloak and a good shirt from Alcinous, and then speaks to Odysseus.

barriers.quote: set a large tripod on the fire
barriers.my_reading: A big metal cauldron standing on three legs, not a camera stand; 'the belly of the tripod' confirms it is a pot.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Arete tells Odysseus to fit the lid himself and tie the chest up at once, so no one can rob him while he sleeps on the ship.

Odysseus puts the lid on the chest and ties it with a knot Circe had taught him, and just then a senior servant calls him to his bath, which he welcomes because no one had looked after him since he left Calypso, who had cared for him like a god. Washed, oiled and dressed in a clean cloak and shirt, he joins the guests at their wine, and lovely Nausicaa, standing by a pillar of the hall, admires him as he passes. She bids him farewell and asks him not to forget her once he is safe at home, since it is to her first that he owes his life.

barriers.quote: a knot that Circe had taught him
barriers.my_reading: Someone from his past travels, apparently a woman, taught him a special knot; who Circe is is never said.

barriers.quote: He had done so before an upper servant told him
barriers.my_reading: He had just finished tying it when a senior servant called him to his bath; it can first read as 'he had done this before, on an earlier occasion'.

barriers.quote: you owe a ransom for having saved your life
barriers.my_reading: You owe me your life, a debt of gratitude; 'ransom' (the price paid to free someone) makes it sound as if she wants payment.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus answers Nausicaa, daughter of Alcinous, that if Zeus, Hera's mighty husband, lets him reach home, he will bless her as his guardian angel all his life, because she saved him.

barriers.quote: my guardian angel
barriers.my_reading: My protector and savior; the meaning is clear, but a Christian image in a world of Greek gods is jarring.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus sits beside Alcinous, supper is served and the wine mixed, and Demodocus is led in and seated in the middle against a pillar of the hall. Odysseus cuts a rich, fatty piece of roast pork from the joint and has a servant take it to Demodocus as a tribute, saying that despite the pain the man's songs cause him, he honors the singer. Bards, he says, are honored everywhere because the Muse teaches them and loves them.

barriers.quote: a piece of roast pork with plenty of fat on it
barriers.my_reading: The fatty cut is the choicest portion, so giving it is an honor; a modern reader may see fat as the worse part.

barriers.quote: abundance left on the joint
barriers.my_reading: Plenty of meat left on the big roast ('joint' = a large cut of meat).

paragraphs.paraphrase: Demodocus is pleased with the pork, and after everyone has eaten, Odysseus praises him above all men, saying he must have been taught by the Muse or by Apollo, since he sings of the Achaeans' return and sufferings as accurately as if he had been there or heard it from someone who was. He asks him to switch to the story of the wooden horse, which Epeus built with Athena's help and which Odysseus got into the fortress of Troy by a trick, packed with the men who then sacked the city, and promises to tell the world of his god-given gift if he sings it truly.

barriers.quote: the return of the Achaeans
barriers.my_reading: The Greeks' war at Troy and their journeys home ('Achaeans' seems to be yet another name for the Greeks); the song in ¶5 was actually about a quarrel, not a return.

barriers.quote: that Odysseus got by stratagem into the fort of Troy
barriers.my_reading: He speaks of himself in the third person because he is still hiding who he is from the Phaeacians.
barriers.note: the text leaves the reader to notice the disguise; for a moment it can seem to be about another man

paragraphs.paraphrase: Inspired by the gods, Demodocus starts where some of the Argives burned their tents and sailed away while others waited with Odysseus hidden inside the horse, which the Trojans had dragged into their fortress and which stood in their meeting place while they argued over whether to smash it, throw it off the cliff, or keep it as an offering to the gods. They chose the last, which doomed the city because the bravest Argives were inside, and the singer tells how the Achaeans burst out of the horse and ravaged the city. Odysseus, raging like Ares, went with Menelaus to the house of Deiphobus, where the fighting was fiercest, and won with Athena's help.

barriers.quote: some of the Argives set fire to their tents and sailed away
barriers.my_reading: Part of the Greek army ('Argives', another name for them) pretended to give up and leave, burning its camp as part of the trick; that it was a pretense is only implied later by 'ambush'.

barriers.quote: And this was how they settled it in the end
barriers.my_reading: 'this' = the last option: they left the horse standing as an offering to the gods.

barriers.quote: along with Menelaus to the house of Deiphobus
barriers.my_reading: Menelaus seems to be a Greek comrade and Deiphobus a Trojan whose house saw the hardest fighting; why that house mattered is not explained.

paragraphs.paraphrase: As Demodocus sings, Odysseus breaks down, his cheeks wet with tears. He weeps like a woman throwing herself on the body of her husband, killed defending his city and children: she screams and clings to him as he dies, while the enemy beat her across the back and shoulders and drag her off to slavery, toil and grief, her beauty fading; that is how pitifully Odysseus weeps. No one notices except Alcinous, who sits close enough to hear his sobs, and he rises at once to speak.

barriers.quote: even so piteously did Odysseus weep
barriers.my_reading: This closes the long comparison: Odysseus weeps as pitifully as that captured widow. After the long detour it is easy to lose the thread, especially read aloud.
barriers.note: the irony that the city-sacker weeps like a sacked city's widow is left to the reader

paragraphs.paraphrase: Alcinous tells the Phaeacian leaders to have Demodocus stop, because ever since the singing began after supper their guest has been groaning and lamenting, clearly in deep distress. The bard should stop so hosts and guest can all enjoy themselves as is proper, since the feast, the voyage home and the gifts are all in the guest's honor, and any decent person treats a guest and suppliant like his own brother.

Alcinous asks the guest in return to stop hiding things and answer plainly: what name did his parents and neighbors call him (everyone has one from birth), and what are his country, people and city, so that the ships can set their course there. Phaeacian ships need no helmsmen or rudders because they understand what their crews are thinking, know every city and land, and cross even fog-bound seas without risk of wreck. Still, Alcinous recalls his father saying that Poseidon resented the Phaeacians for giving everyone passage so freely and threatened one day to wreck one of their ships on its way back from such a voyage and bury their city under a high mountain, though whether the god will do it is up to him.

barriers.quote: do you on your part make no more concealment or reserve
barriers.my_reading: In return, stop hiding things and holding back.

barriers.quote: so that our ships may shape their purpose accordingly
barriers.my_reading: So the ships can set their course and plan accordingly (the ships themselves have minds, as the next sentences say).

barriers.quote: the Phaeacians have no pilots
barriers.my_reading: They have no helmsmen or navigators to steer; not airline pilots.

barriers.quote: too easy-going in the matter of giving people escorts
barriers.my_reading: Too free in carrying anyone and everyone home by ship.
barriers.note: 'escorts' in the plural can sound like the modern escort trade

paragraphs.paraphrase: Alcinous asks him to say truly where he has wandered and which peoples he met, the savage and lawless as well as the hospitable and humane, and why hearing of the return of the Argive Danaans from Troy upsets him so much, since the gods arranged those misfortunes so that later generations would have songs. He asks whether he lost a relative by marriage at Troy, a son-in-law or father-in-law (the closest kin after blood relations), or perhaps a brave and kind comrade, since a good friend is as dear as a brother.

barriers.quote: the return of the Argive Danaans from Troy
barriers.my_reading: The Greeks' war and journey home from Troy; 'Argive Danaans' combines two of the several names used for the Greeks.
barriers.note: Danaans, Achaeans and Argives are never explained

barriers.quote: when you were before Troy
barriers.my_reading: When you were at the siege of Troy, outside its walls; not 'before you went to Troy'.

book_level: The Greeks at Troy go by three unexplained names: Danaans (¶5), Achaeans (¶15, ¶44, ¶45), Argives (¶45), and even 'Argive Danaans' (¶49). The Trojan War background (Agamemnon's prophecy at Pytho, Philoctetes, Epeus, Menelaus, Deiphobus, Heracles, Eurytus, Circe) is assumed; the gist survives, but anything fuller comes from outside knowledge only.

Many words carry older meanings that clash with modern ones: 'escort' (passage home by ship), 'gallery' (the hall), 'couch' (bed), 'toils' (nets), 'copper' and 'tripod' (cauldrons), 'joint' (roast), 'talent' (a weight of gold), 'dart' (javelin), 'pilots' (helmsmen), 'baggage' (a loose woman), 'stouter', 'diverted', 'dressed', 'precincts', 'ransom'.

Archaic idioms and inverted word order slow reading, especially aloud: 'I will find you in everything', 'nothing loath', 'kept no blind lookout', 'made as though', 'foot and trip it', 'cast in heavy damages', 'A bad man's bond is bad security', 'So true is it that...', 'do you on your part make no more concealment', and 'presently' (= soon).
'Aldermen and town councilors' is the stock address to the Phaeacian lords (¶0, ¶2, ¶6, ¶33, ¶47). It sounds like modern local government, and Athena even uses it to ordinary citizens.

Customs are left unexplained: drink offerings and wine mixed with water (¶6, ¶38, ¶43), the fatty cut of pork as an honor, the bride-price Hephaestus wants back, damages for adultery and standing surety (¶23-¶28), why being called a trader is an insult (¶12), and what a 'suppliant' is.

The dramatic irony (the guest is Odysseus, and the Phaeacians do not know it) is never spelled out: he weeps at songs about his own war and asks for a song about 'Odysseus' in the third person (¶44). A reader who missed that he never gave his name in Book 7 may be confused until Alcinous finally asks for it in ¶48.

The Ares-Aphrodite song (¶18-¶29) reads easily, but its relationships are implied rather than stated (Aphrodite as Hephaestus's wife and Zeus's daughter, the Sun as informer), epithets like 'Earth-encircling Poseidon' and 'the givers of all good things' blur who is who, and the legal back-and-forth over Poseidon's guarantee (¶26-¶28) is hard to follow.

Long lists and speeches lose the listener: the roll-call of thirteen athletes (¶7), Odysseus's boast (¶15), Alcinous's quiet backtrack on boxing and wrestling (¶16, contradicting ¶6), the widow simile whose closing line comes after a long detour (¶46), and the speech on self-steering ships and Poseidon's threat (¶48).
